newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU, with warning, backs Helms-Burton peace plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU, with warning, backs Helms-Burton peace plan.

text.p: European Union ambassadors backed a plan on Wednesday to defuse a row with the United States over anti-Cuba legislation, but only after adding a stern warning to Washington not to renege on the deal.

In a sharply worded statement sent to EU capitals for formal approval by Friday, the EU envoys said the bloc would suspend a World Trade Organisation (WTO) disputes panel over the so-called Helms-Burton Act.
But if any action was taken against EU companies or individuals under the Cuba act or a similar one aimed at Iran and Libya, the WTO panel would be restarted.

The statement also repeated the EU's strongly held view that legislation such as Helms-Burton, which threatens foreign companies with certain kinds of dealings in Cuba, are "unacceptable both in law and in principle."

The Helms-Burton legislation, an amalgam of U.S. anti-Cuba laws, has outraged Washington's trading partners because of its so-called extra-territoriality -- its impact on non-U.S. companies doing business outside of the United States.

Since its passage, transatlantic trading relations have been strained and WTO disputes procedures have been threatened with a test that many leading trading countries would like to avoid so early in the organisation's existence.

Seeking to defuse the row, the European Commission and Washington agreed on Friday to negotiate a compromise in policy towards Cuba. The EU would drop its WTO complaint and work with the United States toward a global agreement on protection of expropriated property.
The White House would in exchange seek to change a key provision of Helms-Burton barring executives of companies that invest in disputed properties in Cuba from entering the United States.

But diplomats said that at Wednesday's meeting France, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Belgium insisted that any backing of the deal be accompanied by the threat to reopen the WTO disputes panel if Washington took any action against EU companies.
"The Commission presented member states with a fait accompli," said one diplomat, adding that endorsement in national capitals was by no means automatic.
Spain's ambassador, Javier Elorza, said, however, that he expected approval from the capitals.
"Everyone said they wanted to send the agreement to their governments," Elorza told Reuters after the meeting. "But we know what can fly."

France, indicating that it was not entirely trusting that the United States would stick by the agreement, attached a separate declaration to the statement noting that the threat of extra-territoriality had not been eliminated.

"The French authorities...call on the Commission to excercise the greatest vigilance in the coming months to assure the defence of European interests and to be on watch that the United States makes commitments to guarantee a fair result," it said.
